proposedTopics.title: Types & data locations
proposedTopics.description: Solidity's value types, reference types (arrays/mappings/structs), and the three data locations (storage/memory/calldata) that decide lifetime, copy-vs-alias semantics, and gas.
prerequisiteTitles: The EVM as a state machine

proposedTopics.title: Functions, visibility & modifiers
proposedTopics.description: How functions are declared and controlled: return values, view/pure mutability, the four visibility levels, modifiers, the constructor, and control flow.

proposedTopics.title: Storage layout
proposedTopics.description: How state variables map to 32-byte storage slots: sequential layout, packing, and the constant/immutable escape from storage. This is the foundation for proxies and gas work.

proposedTopics.title: Inheritance
proposedTopics.description: Composing contracts with is, virtual/override, super, shadowing rules, and abstract contracts, plus C3 linearization for multiple inheritance.

proposedTopics.title: Events & logging
proposedTopics.description: Events write to the transaction log — cheap, off-chain-indexable output that contracts themselves cannot read. Indexed topics vs data, and the log's on-chain anatomy.

proposedTopics.title: Value types & their defaults
proposedTopics.description: Value types (bool, uint/int of 8–256 bits, address, bytes1–32, enum) are copied on assignment and every variable starts at a zero value — 0, false, address(0), 0x00…. There is no null: an unset mapping entry or storage slot reads as the type's default, which silently hides 'never set' from 'set to zero'. Since 0.8 arithmetic reverts on overflow/underflow unless wrapped in unchecked.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/Primitives.sol exposing one public var of each value type plus a function that returns the default of an unassigned local, with a Foundry test in test/phase02/Primitives.t.sol asserting each default. Done when: forge test passes and the test proves an unassigned address returns address(0) and an unchecked uint8 wraps 255+1 to 0.

requirements.purpose: Identify Solidity value types and the domains represented by their zero values

proposedTopics.title: Reference types & data location
proposedTopics.description: Arrays, structs and mappings are reference types; bytes and string are special arrays. State variables live in storage, while reference-typed parameters and locals use storage (persistent and a reference when local), memory (a mutable per-call copy), or calldata (read-only input that avoids a memory copy). Assigning a storage local from a storage state var aliases it — writes go to the original, not a copy — which is a classic source of accidental state mutation.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/DataLocations.sol with a function that takes a calldata array, copies it to memory, and mutates a storage struct via a storage-pointer local, with a test in test/phase02/DataLocations.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and the test proves the storage-pointer write persists while the memory copy does not.

proposedTopics.title: Arrays in Solidity
proposedTopics.description: Arrays are fixed-size (uint[3]) or dynamic (uint[]); only dynamic storage arrays support .push/.pop, and memory arrays cannot be resized. delete on an element sets it to zero without shortening the array, leaving a gap. Iterating an unbounded, user-growable array is a DoS footgun: gas grows with length until the transaction can never fit in a block.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/Arrays.sol with push, ordered remove (shift) and gas-cheap unordered remove (swap-and-pop), with a test in test/phase02/Arrays.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts swap-and-pop leaves the array length one shorter and preserves the remaining set.

proposedTopics.title: Mappings
proposedTopics.description: A mapping(K => V) is a hash-table-like store where every possible key already maps to V's default; it lives only in storage and has no length, keys, or iteration. You cannot enumerate a mapping — you must track keys yourself (e.g. a parallel array) if you need to list them. Nested mappings and mappings inside structs work, but deleting the struct does not clear the nested mapping.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/Balances.sol with a mapping(address => uint) plus an enumerable-keys pattern (address[] + mapping(address=>bool) seen), with a test in test/phase02/Balances.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and the test proves an unset key reads 0 and the key list stays deduplicated.

proposedTopics.title: Structs
proposedTopics.description: Structs group named fields into a custom type you can store, pass in memory, or return. You can construct them positionally or with named fields, but a struct that contains a mapping can only exist in storage — you cannot build such a struct in memory. Copying a storage struct to a memory struct duplicates all value fields.

proposedTopics.title: Enums
proposedTopics.description: An enum is a set of named constants represented in the ABI as uint8, defaulting to its first member (index 0) and capped at 256 members. It documents state machines (e.g. Status.Pending/Shipped/Delivered) far more safely than raw integers. Casting an out-of-range integer into an enum reverts with a Panic since 0.8, so enums also validate their own domain.

proposedTopics.title: Ether & Wei units
proposedTopics.description: The EVM counts value in wei; 1 ether = 1e18 wei and 1 gwei = 1e9 wei, with wei/gwei/ether literal suffixes and seconds/minutes/days time suffixes. msg.value and address.balance are always in wei, so forgetting the 18-decimal scale is a pervasive off-by-1e18 bug.

proposedTopics.title: Functions & return values
proposedTopics.description: Functions can return multiple values as a tuple, using either unnamed returns with an explicit return statement or named returns that are pre-declared and can be assigned then implicitly returned. Callers destructure tuples with (a, , c) syntax, skipping fields. An explicit return supplies its expressions directly instead of returning the current named return-variable values, so mixing the two styles is easy to misread.

Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts both return the same tuple and destructuring skips the middle value.

proposedTopics.title: View & pure functions
proposedTopics.description: view promises to read but not modify state; pure promises to neither read nor modify it, and the compiler enforces both. External view calls use STATICCALL, so an on-chain caller cannot smuggle a state change through a normal view call. They cost gas when invoked inside a transaction — a pure/view call simulated off-chain via eth_call consumes no on-chain gas.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/ViewPure.sol with a view getter over state and a pure math function, with a test in test/phase02/ViewPure.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and the contract compiles only because neither function writes state (prove by asserting the getter's value equals the stored value).

requirements.purpose: Separate view and pure compile-time promises from their on-chain call behavior

proposedTopics.title: Visibility specifiers
proposedTopics.description: Functions use public (internal or external calls), external (message calls, including this.f()), internal (this contract and derived contracts), or private (only the declaring contract) visibility. State variables use public, internal, or private, and public state variables receive generated getters. Crucially, private/internal restrict Solidity access only — the data is still readable on-chain, so private is not confidentiality.

Done when: forge test passes and the test calls each externally-reachable function and confirms the private one is not part of the ABI.

proposedTopics.title: Function modifiers
proposedTopics.description: A modifier wraps a function body, splicing it in at the _ placeholder to run code before and/or after — the standard tool for access control (onlyOwner), pausing, and reentrancy guards. A modifier without _ skips the entire function body, and modifier order matters when several apply. Modifiers can take arguments and read function context.

Done when: forge test passes and the test proves a non-owner call reverts and the after-body code runs.

proposedTopics.title: The constructor
proposedTopics.description: The constructor runs exactly once at deployment to initialize state and set immutables, then is discarded — it is not part of the deployed runtime bytecode and can never be called again. It may take arguments (passed in the deploy transaction) and be payable. Base-contract constructors must be given their arguments via the inheritance list or a modifier-style call.

proposedTopics.title: Control flow: conditionals & loops
proposedTopics.description: Solidity has if/else, for, while, do-while, break and continue, but no switch (switch exists only in Yul). Because every step is gas-metered, an unbounded loop over a growable array is a denial-of-service risk once the iteration cost exceeds the block gas limit. Prefer pull-over-push and bounded loops with an explicit cap.

proposedTopics.title: Reading & writing state variables
proposedTopics.description: Persistent state variables live in contract storage; a simple value read compiles to SLOAD and a write to SSTORE, both far pricier than memory. Under the current access-list schedule, the first SLOAD of a slot in a transaction costs 2100 gas and a warm SLOAD costs 100. SSTORE metering depends on the original, current, and new values; setting a warm zero slot to non-zero has a 20000-gas base cost, a first cold touch adds 2100, and eligible clearing can earn a capped refund. Minimizing repeated storage touches is a major gas-optimization lever.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/State.sol with get/set of a uint and a function caching a storage read in a memory local before a loop, with a gas-snapshot test in test/phase02/State.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and the snapshot shows the cached-read version costs less gas than re-reading storage in the loop.

proposedTopics.title: Storage slots & variable packing
proposedTopics.description: State variables are assigned to 32-byte slots sequentially from slot 0, and the compiler packs multiple adjacent small variables (e.g. three uint64 + a bool) when they fit in one slot. Reordering declarations can reduce the number of occupied slots and can combine work when packed fields are read or written together. An isolated write to one packed field still needs a full-slot read-modify-write, so packing can have the opposite gas effect when neighboring fields are usually accessed separately.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/Packing.sol as two structs — one packed (adjacent small types) and one unpacked (a uint256 splitting them) — and set all fields, with a layout assertion and gas snapshot in test/phase02/Packing.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes, the test proves the packed layout occupies fewer slots, and the snapshot records gas without assuming every packed access is cheaper.

proposedTopics.title: constant vs immutable
proposedTopics.description: constant values are fixed at compile time and substituted at every use — they occupy no storage slot and must be known before deployment. immutable values can be assigned during construction and are substituted into the deployed runtime code, also using no storage slot, but they can depend on constructor arguments. Both are much cheaper to read than a storage variable, though a constant can sometimes be cheaper than an immutable.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/Consts.sol with a constant MAX and an immutable owner set from a constructor arg, plus a storage equivalent, with a gas-snapshot test in test/phase02/Consts.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and the snapshot shows reading constant/immutable is cheaper than reading the storage version.

proposedTopics.title: Inheritance & function overriding
proposedTopics.description: A contract inherits with is, and a base function can be overridden only if it is marked virtual and the child marks override. With multiple inheritance, an explicit override list names the relevant bases unless a documented common-base exception applies. Solidity uses C3 linearization: direct bases are listed from most base-like to most derived, while function lookup searches the listed bases right-to-left. Getting virtual/override wrong is a compile error, but reordering bases can change which implementation runs.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/Inherit.sol with A, B is A, C is A, and D is B, C overriding a virtual foo(), with a test in test/phase02/Inherit.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts D().foo() resolves through the C3 order you predicted.

proposedTopics.title: Calling parent contracts (super)
proposedTopics.description: You can invoke an overridden parent function directly by name (Base.foo()) or via super.foo(), which follows the C3-linearized chain rather than a single literal parent. In a diamond, super calls the next contract in the final inheritance order, not necessarily a base named directly in the current contract's is list; this is how cooperative hook chains can reach every mixin once.

Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts the concatenation order matches the C3 linearization, not the declaration order.

proposedTopics.title: Shadowing inherited state variables
proposedTopics.description: Since 0.6 a child cannot redeclare a visible inherited state variable; it must assign the inherited variable instead, and a redeclaration is a compile error. A private base variable is not visible to the child, so the current rule permits the child to use the same name for a distinct variable. Local variables may still shadow state variables, which compiles with a warning and is a readability and audit hazard.

Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts the single inherited variable reflects the child's assignment.

proposedTopics.title: Abstract contracts & virtual functions
proposedTopics.description: A contract must be abstract if it has an unimplemented function or does not supply every required base-constructor argument, and a fully implemented contract may also be declared abstract intentionally. Abstract contracts cannot be deployed directly. They can hold state, constructors, and implemented functions — unlike interfaces, which cannot declare state variables or constructors and cannot implement functions. Abstract contracts are the base-class tool for shared logic with pluggable pieces.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase02/Abstract.sol with an abstract Base declaring a virtual fee() and shared logic, and a concrete Child implementing fee(), with a test in test/phase02/Abstract.t.sol. Done when: forge test passes and the test deploys only Child and asserts the shared logic uses Child's fee().

proposedTopics.title: Events & indexed topics
proposedTopics.description: emit writes an event to the transaction log — the standard way to surface state changes to off-chain indexers and UIs. A non-anonymous event may index up to three parameters, making them filterable topics, while the rest are ABI-encoded into the log's data. Indexing a dynamic or otherwise complex type stores a Keccak-256 hash of its special in-place encoding, so the original value cannot be decoded from the topic alone.

Done when: forge test passes and the test asserts the emitted topics and data match the expected event.

proposedTopics.title: Log anatomy: topics vs data
proposedTopics.description: A log entry has up to four 32-byte topics plus a data byte array. For a normal event, topic0 is keccak256 of the canonical event signature and the remaining topics represent indexed arguments; non-indexed arguments are ABI-encoded into data. An anonymous event omits topic0, freeing a fourth indexed slot but preventing filtering by an event-signature topic. Contracts cannot read logs directly — logs are output for off-chain consumers.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What value does an unassigned Solidity variable hold, and how does 0.8 treat integer overflow?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Every type has a zero default: uint/int→0, bool→false, address→address(0), bytesN→zeroes. Since 0.8 arithmetic reverts on over/underflow unless wrapped in unchecked. Pitfall: there is no null — 'unset' and 'set to zero' are indistinguishable, so a zero balance can't be told from a missing one.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the three data locations, and what happens when you assign a storage state variable to a storage local?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: storage (persistent; a reference when local), memory (a mutable per-call copy), calldata (read-only input that avoids a memory copy). A storage local aliases the original — writes hit the state var, not a copy. Pitfall: expecting a copy and getting an alias silently mutates state.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is iterating a user-growable array dangerous, and what does delete do to an element?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Loop gas grows with length, so an unbounded array can exceed the block gas limit and brick the function (DoS). delete zeroes the element without shrinking length. Pitfall: use swap-and-pop for O(1) removal and never loop over attacker-growable arrays.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write an O(1) unordered remove for a storage uint[] arr at index i.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: arr[i] = arr[arr.length - 1]; arr.pop(); — overwrite the target with the last element, then pop. Order is not preserved.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why can't you get a mapping's length or iterate it, and what breaks when a mapping is nested in a struct you delete?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A mapping is a pure key→slot hash with no stored key set, so there's no length or enumeration — track keys yourself. Pitfall: delete of a struct does NOT clear a mapping inside it; those entries persist and must be cleared by key.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a mapping-based balance store with a deposit that credits the sender.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: mapping(address => uint256) public balanceOf; function deposit() external payable { balanceOf[msg.sender] += msg.value; }

proposedPrompts.promptText: What restriction applies to a struct that contains a mapping?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It can only exist in storage — you cannot instantiate or pass such a struct in memory. Pitfall: trying to build a memory struct that has a mapping field is a compile error; copy field-by-field or keep the mapping outside.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is an enum's default value and backing type, and what happens on an out-of-range cast?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The ABI represents an enum as uint8; its default is the first member (index 0), and it has at most 256 members. Casting an out-of-range integer to the enum reverts with a Panic since 0.8. Pitfall: relying on a 'zero = unset' sentinel is impossible — index 0 is a real, valid member.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How many wei is 1 ether, and what unit are msg.value and address.balance in?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: 1 ether = 1e18 wei; 1 gwei = 1e9 wei. msg.value and balances are always in wei. Pitfall: mixing 'human' ether with raw wei is an off-by-1e18 error — always scale explicitly.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do named returns differ from an explicit return, and how does a caller take just the third of three returns?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Named returns pre-declare variables that can be assigned and implicitly returned; an explicit return supplies its expressions directly. Destructure with (, , c) = f(); to skip fields. Pitfall: mixing implicit named returns with explicit return expressions is easy to misread.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does view promise versus pure, and are they free to call?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: view reads state but never writes; pure neither reads nor writes; the compiler enforces both, and external view calls use STATICCALL. Free only via off-chain eth_call — inside a transaction they still cost gas. Pitfall: view doesn't mean gasless when reached on-chain.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Name the four visibility levels and correct the myth that private data is hidden.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Functions can be public (internal or external calls), external (message calls, including this.f()), internal (this contract and derived contracts), or private (only the declaring contract). State variables use public, internal, or private; public variables receive generated getters. Pitfall: private/internal restrict Solidity access only — storage remains readable on-chain.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does the _ in a modifier do, and what happens if it's missing?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: _ marks where the wrapped function body executes; code before/after _ runs around it. Pitfall: a modifier with no _ silently skips the entire function body (the call succeeds but does nothing) — and when several modifiers apply, their order matters.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write an onlyOwner modifier using a custom error.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: error NotOwner(); modifier onlyOwner() { if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner(); _; }

proposedPrompts.promptText: When does the constructor run, and why can't it be called later?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Once, during deployment, to init state and set immutables; it's part of the creation code, not the deployed runtime bytecode, so it no longer exists to call. Pitfall: forgetting to initialize an owner/immutable in the constructor leaves it at its zero default with no second chance.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Which control-flow construct does Solidity NOT have, and what's the danger of loops?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: No switch (that's Yul-only); it has if/else, for, while, do-while, break, continue. Pitfall: an unbounded loop over an attacker-growable array can exceed the block gas limit and permanently DoS the function — bound loops or use pull payments.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Compare the gas of a cold SLOAD, a warm SLOAD, and a zero→non-zero SSTORE.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A cold SLOAD costs 2100 gas and a warm SLOAD 100. A warm zero→non-zero SSTORE has a 20000-gas base cost; a first cold touch adds 2100. Other SSTORE costs depend on the original, current, and new values, and eligible refunds are capped. Pitfall: cache repeated storage reads in a local.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a loop that sums a storage uint[] without re-reading the array length from storage each iteration.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 len = arr.length; uint256 s; for (uint256 i; i < len; ++i) { s += arr[i]; } — cache length in a local so the loop test doesn't SLOAD each time.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does the compiler pack state variables, and when does packing NOT help?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It lays variables out sequentially from slot 0 and packs adjacent sub-32-byte types into one slot. Packing reduces occupied slots and can combine work when neighboring fields are accessed together. Pitfall: writing one packed field alone requires a full-slot read-modify-write, so packing separately accessed fields can cost more.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do constant and immutable differ, and what do they share?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: constant is fixed at compile time and substituted at each use; immutable can be assigned during construction from values such as constructor arguments and is substituted into runtime code. Neither occupies a storage slot, though a constant can sometimes be cheaper. Pitfall: an immutable cannot be assigned after construction.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What must a base and child mark to override, and how is multiple inheritance resolved?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Base marks virtual and child marks override. With multiple inheritance, the override list names the relevant bases unless the documented common-base exception applies. Direct bases are declared from most base-like to most derived, and lookup searches them right-to-left. Pitfall: reordering bases can change resolution.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the signature of a child function that overrides a foo() declared virtual in both A and B.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function foo() public override(A, B) { ... } — when both A and B independently declare foo, the override list names both; Solidity documents an exception when one base inherits the declaring function from another.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does super.foo() choose which parent runs in a diamond hierarchy?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It calls the next contract in the C3-linearized method resolution order, not a single literal parent — so a chain of super calls walks every mixin once. Pitfall: assuming super means 'my declared parent' breaks in multiple inheritance; trace the MRO.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Can a child redeclare an inherited state variable? How should it set the base's value?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A child cannot redeclare a visible inherited state variable; assign that inherited variable directly. A private base variable is not visible, so the child may use the same name for a distinct variable. Pitfall: local variables can shadow state variables and compile with a warning.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes a contract abstract, and how does it differ from an interface?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A contract must be abstract if it has an unimplemented function or lacks required base-constructor arguments; a fully implemented contract may also be marked abstract intentionally. It cannot be deployed directly. Unlike an interface, it may hold state, constructors, and implemented functions.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How many event parameters can be indexed, and what is lost by indexing a string?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A non-anonymous event may index up to three parameters; an anonymous event may index four. The rest go into ABI-encoded data. Pitfall: an indexed dynamic or complex value stores Keccak-256 of its special in-place encoding, so the original is not decodable from the topic alone.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write an ERC-20-style Transfer event declaration with the correct indexing.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value); — addresses indexed for filtering, value in data.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is topic0 of a normal event, and what changes for an anonymous event? Can a contract read logs?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: topic0 = keccak256 of the event signature; indexed args fill topics 1–3, non-indexed args go in data. An anonymous event omits topic0 (gaining a 4th indexed slot) but is unfilterable by signature. Pitfall: contracts cannot read logs at all — logs are output for off-chain consumers only.
